summary: Specifies the Binary Floor Control Protocol, used to manage joint or exclusive access to shared resources in a conference. Floor control complements conference setup, media control and policy protocols. It was standards-track and has been replaced by RFC 8855.

eli5.summary: In a meeting only one person talks at a time. BFCP is the way people raise a hand and a chair gives them the floor.

questions: how to manage who speaks in a conference
subtitle: A compact binary protocol for deciding who gets to use a shared resource, such as the right to talk, in a conference.

tldr.problem: In a multiparty conference some resources, such as the right to send media to a session, must be shared or held exclusively, and someone has to coordinate who gets them.
tldr.mechanism: Floor participants send requests to a floor control server over TCP. The server can ask floor chairs for decisions, grants or denies the floor, and keeps everyone informed, using a small TLV-encoded binary message format protected by TLS.
tldr.outcome: BFCP only arbitrates access to floors; creating floors and the rules for granting them are handled elsewhere. This RFC has been obsoleted by RFC 8855.

today: RFC 4582 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 8855 and was updated by RFC 8996. Use RFC 8855 for the current BFCP specification.

sections.title: What Floor Control Does
sections.content:
Within a conference, some applications need to manage access to shared resources, such as the right to send media to a particular media session. A floor is a temporary permission to access or manipulate such a resource, and floor control gives users coordinated, shared or exclusive access to it.

BFCP is designed to work in low-bandwidth environments. Its binary encoding keeps messages small (when signatures are not used) so delay-sensitive messages such as FloorRequest, FloorRelease, FloorRequestStatus and ChairAction are quick to send.

Three roles take part. A floor participant asks for floors. A floor chair is a moderator who grants, denies or revokes a floor. The floor control server holds the state of all floors and has the final say on keeping that state coherent. Roles are defined per transaction, so one entity can act as a chair in one exchange and a participant in another.
sections.eli5: Think of a talking stick. Whoever holds it may speak. BFCP is how you ask for the stick and how the teacher decides who gets it next.

sections.title: What Is Out of Scope
sections.content:
BFCP only arbitrates access to floors. It lets participants send floor requests, lets servers grant or deny them, lets chairs pass decisions to the server, and keeps participants and chairs informed.

Several related tasks are done by other mechanisms. Creating and ending floors, and linking a floor to the resources it controls, are handled by the conference control protocol that manipulates the conference object. Clients can learn the server address, conference identifier and user identifier from an SDP offer/answer exchange or other means in the XCON framework. The rules for how floors are granted are also left to other protocols.

Holding a floor gives the right to use the associated resource, but it does not by itself stop others from using the resource.
sections.eli5: BFCP only handles who gets a turn. Deciding what the turns are for, or who is in the room, is somebody else's job.

sections.title: How a Floor Request Works
sections.content:
A participant sends a FloorRequest with one or more FLOOR-ID attributes. If it lists several floors, the server treats them as an atomic package and grants or denies all of them. A third-party request names the beneficiary in a BENEFICIARY-ID attribute, for the case where the sender is not the participant who will get the floor.

The server answers with FloorRequestStatus messages. The first one has the same Transaction ID as the request and carries a new Floor Request ID in a FLOOR-REQUEST-INFORMATION attribute. Later updates carry the same Floor Request ID and use Transaction ID 0. A request moves through values such as Pending, Accepted, Granted, Denied, Cancelled, Released and Revoked. Pending means the server still needs to contact a chair.

Chairs send a ChairAction message to say what they want, and the server answers with ChairActionAck. The server must weigh these instructions against its own state: for instance, it will not grant a multi-floor request until all the responsible chairs agree, and it may have to revoke a floor from its current holder first. Clients can also ask about floors, floor requests and users with query messages.
sections.eli5: You raise your hand and are told you are waiting. The teacher says yes, you talk, and when you are done you say you are finished.

sections.title: Message and Attribute Format
sections.content:
Every BFCP message begins with a 12-octet common header followed by attributes, all in network byte order. The header has a 3-bit version (set to 1), a reserved field, an 8-bit primitive, a 16-bit payload length counted in 4-octet units, a 32-bit Conference ID, a 16-bit Transaction ID and a 16-bit User ID.

Attributes are Type-Length-Value, 32-bit aligned. A 7-bit type is followed by an M (mandatory) bit and an 8-bit length. An unrecognized attribute with M set causes the message to be rejected, otherwise it is ignored. The defined attributes (types 1 to 18) use formats Unsigned16, OctetString16, OctetString and Grouped; grouped attributes contain other attributes.

There are 13 primitives. FloorRequest, FloorRelease, FloorRequestQuery, UserQuery, FloorQuery, ChairAction and Hello go to the server, which replies with FloorRequestStatus, UserStatus, FloorStatus, ChairActionAck, HelloAck or Error.
sections.eli5: Each message starts with a small label saying what it is, which meeting it belongs to and who sent it. Extra details come after, each one in its own little box.

sections.title: Transport and Security
sections.content:
BFCP runs over TCP. TCP provides a byte stream, so BFCP does its own framing with TLV attributes. A client must not use more than one TCP connection to a given floor control server within a conference. If data cannot be parsed, the entity must close the connection, and it should be reestablished. If a connection is lost, the server should keep the participant's floor requests while it is reestablished.

Clients and servers must support TLS, and at a minimum the ciphersuite TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA. Both sides should authenticate each other, with TLS mutual authentication recommended, relying on self-signed certificates or their fingerprints exchanged over an integrity-protected channel. A server that receives a message over plain TCP can answer with Error Code 9 (Use TLS). Messages from a client that cannot be authorized must not be processed further.

The RFC recommends TLS with non-null encryption. Authentication blocks impersonation of clients and servers, TLS integrity protection blocks modification, and checking that the User ID is authorized for that connection blocks replay.
sections.eli5: Everyone shows an ID at the door and talks through a sealed tube, so nobody can pretend to be the teacher or change the notes in transit.

fields.desc: Set to zero by the sender and ignored by the receiver.

fields.desc: Length in 4-octet units, excluding the common header.

fields.desc: Matches a response to its request; 0 in server-initiated transactions.

fields.desc: Uniquely identifies a participant within a conference.
